indiaMissions/india-diamper-coonan-cross: Synod of Diamper (1599) and the Coonan Cross Oath (1653)
Udayamperoor (Diamper), Kerala

In June 1599 Archbishop Alexis de Menezes of Goa convened the Synod of Diamper, which cut the St Thomas Christians off from the Church of the East, condemned 'Nestorian' teaching, burned or expurgated Syriac books and imposed Latin discipline under Jesuit bishops. Half a century of resentment exploded in the Coonan Cross Oath of 3 January 1653, when thousands swore at Mattancherry never to obey the Jesuits. Rome's Carmelite envoys won most parishes back, but the remainder formed an independent church that joined the Syriac Orthodox tradition in 1665 — the origin of the lasting division between Kerala's Catholic and Orthodox Syrian Christians.

The Portuguese regarded the St Thomas Christians as fellow Christians tainted by 'Nestorianism' — loyalty to the Church of the East, whose theology the Council of Ephesus (431) had condemned. When the last East Syriac metropolitan, Mar Abraham, died in 1597, Alexis de Menezes, the Augustinian archbishop of Goa, saw his chance. Early in 1599 he toured the Syrian parishes with Portuguese backing, ordaining dozens of new priests to win their loyalty and pressing the archdeacon, George of the Cross, to submit. He then summoned a synod to Udayamperoor (Diamper), near Cochin, which met from 20 to 26 June 1599 with 153 priests and some 660 lay representatives.

The synod's decrees, drafted in Portuguese and read in Malayalam translation, transformed the church. It condemned Nestorius, removed the name of the 'Patriarch of Babylon' from the liturgy and required submission to the Pope and the Padroado. Syriac books judged heretical were to be surrendered and corrected or burned; the East Syriac Qurbana was revised to conform to Latin doctrine; the veneration of East Syriac saints was forbidden. Priests, who had commonly married, were required to be celibate; the Tridentine sacraments of confirmation and auricular confession were imposed; and many customs shared with Hindu neighbours — astrology, certain marriage practices and ritual pollution beliefs — were condemned, though the synod left caste distinctions largely untouched. In 1600 Rome placed the community under Latin Jesuit bishops at Angamaly, a see transferred to Cranganore in 1605, beginning with Francisco Ros (1601–1624).

For half a century the archdeacons resisted the Jesuit bishops' attempts to govern without them. Under Bishop Francisco Garcia (1641–1659) relations broke down completely. In 1652 a bishop from the Middle East named Ahatallah, who claimed to have been sent by the patriarch, arrived at Mylapore; the Portuguese seized him and shipped him to Goa, and rumours spread in Kerala that he had been drowned in Cochin harbour. On 3 January 1653 a great crowd of Thomas Christians gathered at the church of Our Lady of Life in Mattancherry. Unable all to touch the stone cross, they tied ropes to it and swore together that they would no longer obey Garcia or the Jesuits. Tradition holds that the cross bent under the strain — hence 'Coonan Cross' (koonan kurishu, the 'leaning cross'). On 22 May 1653 at Alangad twelve priests laid hands on Archdeacon Thomas (Parambil Thomas), proclaiming him bishop as Mar Thoma I.

Rome responded by sending Italian Discalced Carmelites under the authority of Propaganda Fide rather than the Portuguese Jesuits. Led by Joseph Sebastiani, they persuaded many to return to Catholic communion, arguing that Mar Thoma I's consecration was invalid. When the Dutch East India Company captured Cochin in January 1663 and expelled Catholic missionaries, Sebastiani consecrated an Indian, Parambil Chandy (Alexander de Campo), as vicar apostolic. By then 84 of the 116 communities had returned to Rome, while 32 remained with Mar Thoma I. In 1665 the Syriac Orthodox bishop Mar Gregorios Abdul Jaleel of Jerusalem arrived and recognised Mar Thoma I, and over the following century the independent party adopted the West Syriac (Antiochene) liturgy and miaphysite Christology.

The events created the enduring division of the Thomas Christians into the Pazhayakoor ('old allegiance', the Catholic Syro-Malabar Church) and the Puthenkoor ('new allegiance', the Malankara churches). The Catholic party remained under Latin bishops — Carmelites and Padroado prelates — until Rome created vicariates apostolic for them under Indian bishops in 1896 and a full hierarchy in 1923. Latinisation itself became a long-running issue: twentieth-century scholars and bishops sought to restore East Syriac elements of the liturgy, and disputes over the form of the Qurbana led to open conflict in the Archdiocese of Ernakulam-Angamaly between 2021 and 2024. On the Puthenkoor side, the question of who held authority — a Kerala metropolitan or the patriarch of Antioch — underlay the later Orthodox–Jacobite division.

Diamper and the Coonan Cross Oath are the defining trauma and the defining act of resistance in Kerala Christianity. They show how a European church, backed by an empire, tried to remake an older Asian church in its own image, and how that church answered — by an oath of collective dissent that is still remembered as an assertion of Indian Christian self-determination.

indiaMissions/india-tranquebar/title: Tranquebar: Ziegenbalg, Plütschau and the first Protestant mission
indiaMissions/india-tranquebar/summary: On 9 July 1706 two young German Lutherans trained at Halle, Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau, landed at the Danish trading post of Tranquebar, sent by King Frederik IV of Denmark. They began the first organised Protestant mission in India, with a pietist emphasis on the vernacular Bible, schools, print and the study of Tamil religion. Ziegenbalg's Tamil New Testament (1714–15) was the first printed Bible translation in any Indian language, and the Tranquebar mission became the root of Tamil Lutheranism and a model for the Protestant missionary movement.
indiaMissions/india-tranquebar/story:
Denmark had held Tranquebar since 1620, with Fort Dansborg protecting a small trading settlement, but its chaplains served only Europeans. In 1705 King Frederik IV, prompted by his court chaplain Franz Julius Lütkens, resolved to send missionaries. Finding no willing Danes, Lütkens recruited two Germans from the circle of August Hermann Francke at Halle: Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg (born 1682 in Pulsnitz, Saxony) and Heinrich Plütschau (born 1677 in Mecklenburg). They sailed from Copenhagen in November 1705 and reached Tranquebar on 9 July 1706. The Danish commandant, J. S. Hassius, and the Danish East India Company saw them as troublemakers; in 1708–09 Ziegenbalg was imprisoned for four months.

Ziegenbalg set out to learn Tamil by sitting with the children of a village school, tracing letters in the sand. Within a few years he was preaching, writing and translating. The first baptisms, of five slaves of Danish households, took place on 12 May 1707, and the Jerusalem church was consecrated that August; the larger New Jerusalem Church followed in 1718. The missionaries opened schools for boys and girls — among the first in South India to teach girls to read — and a seminary for catechists and teachers. In 1712 the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge (SPCK) in London sent a printing press, and with Tamil type cast in Halle the mission printed the Tamil New Testament (1714–15) along with catechisms, hymnals and grammars. Benjamin Schultze completed the Old Testament in 1727–28.

Ziegenbalg was also a serious student of Tamil religion and society. He collected palm-leaf manuscripts, compiled the Bibliotheca Malabarica (1708), a catalogue of Tamil books, and held public dialogues with Hindu and Muslim scholars, later published in Europe. His Genealogy of the South Indian Gods (1713) was considered too sympathetic to 'heathenism' by Francke, who refused to print it; it was published only in 1867. The Halle Reports (Hallesche Berichte), published from 1710, circulated the mission's letters across Protestant Europe and inspired Count Zinzendorf, who met Ziegenbalg in 1715, and the later British missionary societies. Ziegenbalg travelled to Europe in 1714–16, where he met George I in London, before returning to Tranquebar. Worn out by work and conflict with the mission board in Copenhagen, he died on 23 February 1719 at the age of thirty-six, leaving a congregation of some 250 baptised Christians; Plütschau had returned to Europe in 1711, and Johann Ernst Gründler died in 1720.

The mission continued under Halle-trained successors for more than a century. It ordained the first Indian Lutheran pastor, Aaron, in 1733, followed by Diogo and others; extended its work to Madras (Vepery, 1726), Cuddalore (1737), Thanjavur and Tiruchirappalli; and through the SPCK became an unusual partnership between German Lutheran missionaries and the Church of England. Its most famous later missionary, Christian Friedrich Schwartz, arrived in 1750 and became a confidant of the rulers of Thanjavur. Moravian Brethren also maintained a settlement, the 'Brethren's Garden', at Tranquebar from 1760 to 1803.

The mission struggled with caste from the start. Converts came from many backgrounds, including Vellalars, Paraiyars and Pallars, and the missionaries allowed separate seating and separate communion cups for caste and Dalit Christians to avoid losing high-caste members — a compromise later attacked by evangelical missionaries and defended by the Leipzig Mission in the 'caste controversy' of the 1840s–50s. By the late eighteenth century rationalism at Halle, war and lack of funds had weakened the mission. Denmark sold Tranquebar to the British East India Company in 1845, and in 1847 the Leipzig Evangelical Lutheran Mission took over the Tamil congregations, which became the Tamil Evangelical Lutheran Church in 1919.

indiaMissions/india-tranquebar/legacy: Tranquebar was the beginning of Protestant mission in India and arguably of the modern Protestant missionary movement. Its commitments to vernacular Scripture, literacy, print, schools and serious study of Indian religion became the standard Protestant pattern, while its compromise over caste foreshadowed one of the most persistent problems of Indian Christianity.
